definition: An address used by a program within an address-space context. Ordinary memory accesses are translated by the MMU; the same numeric virtual address can name different backing in different processes.
example: Two processes can both use virtual address 0x4000 and reach different physical memory.

definition: Making a program work when it is loaded at a different address from the one it was built for, either by patching its addresses or by translating them in hardware.
example: Base-and-bounds hardware relocates a process loaded at 32 KiB by adding 32,768 to every address.

definition: An ordinary x86-64 linear address whose high bits match the sign extension of the highest implemented linear-address bit: bit 47 with four-level paging or bit 56 with five levels. Address-tag masking features add rules; an invalid ordinary canonical form faults rather than selecting a page-table entry.
example: 0x00007fffffffffff is canonical; 0x0000800000000000 is not.

definition: A way to learn secret data from indirect effects, such as how long a memory access takes, rather than reading it directly.

The simplest hardware address translation: a base register holds where the process starts in physical memory and a bounds register holds its size. Each address is checked against the bounds and then has the base added.
example: With base 40,000 and bounds 8,000, virtual 5,000 becomes physical 45,000 and virtual 8,000 faults.

definition: Dividing a process's memory into variable-sized logical segments (code, heap, stack) each with its own base, size and protection, so each can be placed in RAM independently. It suffers external fragmentation.

A table recording segment bases, sizes and permissions in a segmented memory model. Protected-mode x86 segment selectors identify descriptors; original 8086 segment registers instead contribute directly to real-mode address arithmetic.

The Unix bus-error signal. Linux can deliver SIGBUS for an access to a mapped whole page beyond a file’s end, or for an unresolvable backing-object error; not every file-tail access or storage error has identical behaviour.
example: Touching a mapped page beyond the end of a file that was truncated to 0 bytes delivers SIGBUS.

definition: Flags on a segment or page saying whether it may be read, written or executed, and whether user mode may touch it. The hardware checks them on every access.
Free memory broken into scattered holes between allocations, so a large request fails even though enough memory is free in total.
example: Holes of 30, 25 and 40 MiB cannot hold a 60 MiB segment despite 95 MiB being free.

definition: Memory wasted inside an allocated block because the request was rounded up to the block's size.
example: A 100-byte malloc that gets a 112-byte chunk wastes 12 bytes internally.

definition: Moving suitable allocations or physical pages to make larger contiguous free ranges. Linux memory compaction can help satisfy high-order and huge-page allocations, but its success and latency depend on movable pages, fragmentation and policy.
Intel’s 1978 16-bit processor, which combines a segment value shifted left four bits with an offset. The original twenty physical address bits cover 1 MiB and discard carry beyond that range.
Intel's 1982 processor that added protected mode, with segment descriptors holding a base, a limit and a privilege level.
Intel's 1985 32-bit processor that added paging underneath segmentation; 32-bit Linux relies mainly on its paging.

The legacy x86 mode using segment-and-offset addressing rather than protected-mode segment descriptors. The original 8086 exposed twenty address bits; later processors can enable an additional address bit and change wrapping behaviour, so real mode is not universally a twenty-bit physical-address limit.
The x86 mode, introduced with the 80286, that adds memory protection and privilege levels through segment descriptors, and on the 80386 paging.

The x86-64 mode containing a native 64-bit submode and a compatibility submode for older code. Paging is required; ordinary segment bases and limits are mostly ignored in native 64-bit execution, while compatibility execution retains different segmentation rules.
Basic Input/Output System: the firmware older PCs run at power-on. In real mode its interrupt vector table sat at physical address 0.
A variant of fork in which the child borrows the parent's memory until it calls exec or exits, with strict limits on what it may do.
A page fault caused by writing to a page shared copy-on-write. The kernel copies the page for the writer (or, if no one else still shares it, just makes it writable) and retries the write.
example: After fork, a parent writing 50 MiB of pages copies just those 50 MiB.

definition: Mapping a virtual-address range, either backed by a file or anonymous zero-filled memory. Ordinary file mappings generally use page-cache backing; private modifications do not update the file, while shared mappings have different visibility and synchronization rules.
The system call that changes the read, write and execute permissions of mapped pages.

Memory-advice operations include MADV_DONTNEED to discard eligible mapping backing, MADV_COLLAPSE to request synchronous huge-page collapse, and MADV_DONTFORK or MADV_WIPEONFORK to change child inheritance. These operations have distinct rules and support requirements.

Linux calls for keeping eligible mapped pages resident, subject to limits and successful completion. mlock2 with MLOCK_ONFAULT delays locking until pages are touched; locking does not prevent every later protection or copy-on-write fault.
A system call that writes modified pages of a shared file mapping back to the file; with MS_SYNC it waits for the write to finish.

A call requesting that a file’s modified data and required metadata reach the storage device, and waiting for completion. Durability still depends on successful error handling, filesystem and hardware guarantees; creating or renaming a file can also require syncing its directory.
An mmap flag for memory with no file behind it; it starts zero-filled.
An mmap flag requesting prefaulting and, for file mappings, read-ahead. mmap can still succeed without fully populating the range, and future eviction or copy-on-write can cause more faults.
A file listing every mapping of a process: address range, permissions (such as r-xp or rw-p) and what backs it.
The x86 exception for many protection violations, including using a non-canonical address. Stack accesses to a non-canonical address raise a stack-segment fault instead.
Filling the upper bits of a number with copies of its top bit. x86-64 canonical addresses are the 48-bit (or 57-bit) address sign-extended to 64 bits.
Storing extra information in a pointer's unused high bits, which hardware features can mask off before translation. It is why Linux avoids handing out addresses above 47 bits by default.

Dividing virtual addresses into fixed-size pages and managing suitable physical backing in corresponding frames. Ordinary virtual pages need not occupy one contiguous physical range; page size, permissions, hardware and allocation constraints still apply.
Virtual page number: the high bits of a virtual address, saying which page it falls in. Translation replaces it with a frame number.
example: With 4 KiB pages, address 0x3A7C has VPN 0x3.

definition: Physical frame number: which frame of RAM holds a page. The physical address is the PFN times the page size plus the offset.
The low bits of an address, giving the byte's position inside its page; 12 bits for 4 KiB pages. Translation leaves it unchanged.
example: Address 0x3A7C has offset 0xA7C within its 4 KiB page.

definition: Page table entry: one record in a page table, holding a frame number and flag bits such as present, writable, user, accessed, dirty and no-execute. On x86-64 it is 8 bytes.

The x86 page-table flag indicating a present mapping or next-level table. A clear flag normally makes an access fault; the OS can encode software state such as swap information while respecting architectural and security constraints.

A hardware-maintained page-table access flag used as evidence of translation use. Software that clears it must follow the required invalidation protocol; a cached translation does not guarantee a fresh memory update on every later access.

A hardware-maintained page-table flag indicating a write through the mapping. Whether backing must be written before reclaim depends on its kind and whether the contents must be preserved; discarding unneeded data differs from preserving dirty file or anonymous contents.

A page with modified contents relevant to its backing or tracking context. Preserving dirty file contents normally requires writeback before dropping the frame; live migration must account for pages changed since an earlier copy. Explicitly discarding unneeded contents is a different operation.
A page whose contents still match the copy on storage, so the kernel can drop it without writing and reread it later.
No-execute: a PTE flag (bit 63 on x86-64) that makes instruction fetches from the page fault, so data and stack memory cannot be run as code.

The x86 page-table write-permission flag. Ordinary user-mode writes require effective write permission at all relevant levels; supervisor write protection also depends on control state, and changed permissions need appropriate translation invalidation.
The x86 PTE flag (bit 2) that allows user-mode access. With it clear the page is supervisor-only.

An x86 translation marked global when global-page support is enabled. It can survive ordinary CR3 changes, unlike translations subject to that change’s invalidation rules; explicit invalidation and architectural exceptions still apply.
The page-size flag in an x86-64 PD or PDPT entry. When set, the entry maps a 2 MiB or 1 GiB huge page directly and the walk stops early.
The number of physical-address bits a particular x86 CPU implements, up to 52. It limits which PTE bits hold the frame address.

A page table stored as a tree: the top table points to lower tables, which are allocated only for regions in use. It saves a great deal of memory for sparse address spaces at the cost of more reads per walk.
example: Four-level x86-64 paging uses four levels of 512-entry tables, each indexed by nine address bits. Five-level mode adds another level.

definition: One array containing an entry for every possible virtual page. In the lesson’s 48-bit address, 4 KiB page and eight-byte entry model, the full table occupies 512 GiB, including unused pages.
Page map level 4: the top table of x86-64 4-level paging. Each of its 512 entries covers 512 GiB; CR3 points at it.
The extra top table added by x86-64 5-level paging, above PML4.
Page directory pointer table: the second level of x86-64 4-level paging. Each entry covers 1 GiB, or maps a 1 GiB page directly.
Page directory: the third level of x86-64 4-level paging. Each entry covers 2 MiB by pointing to a PT, or maps a 2 MiB huge page directly.
The lowest (leaf) level of x86-64 paging: a 4 KiB table of 512 PTEs, each mapping one 4 KiB page, so one PT maps 2 MiB.
Page global directory: Linux's name for the top level of a process's page tables (PML4, or PML5 with 5-level paging).
Linux's name for the page-table level that is PML4 under 5-level paging. With 4 levels it is 'folded' away into the PGD.
Page upper directory: Linux's name for the x86-64 PDPT level.
Page middle directory: Linux's name for the x86-64 PD level; a PMD-sized page is 2 MiB on x86-64.
The x86 control register into which the CPU puts the faulting virtual address when it raises a page fault.
Following the page-table tree from the root to the entry for one address. On x86-64 with 4 levels, an uncached walk reads four entries; the hardware page walker does it on a TLB miss.
Small CPU caches of upper-level page-table entries, letting a TLB miss skip some levels of the walk.

A translation structure with entries associated with physical frames rather than every possible virtual page. Lookup may use a hash over address-space identity and virtual page number; a hashed forward mapping table is not automatically an inverted table.

The base-page granule selected for ARM64 translation: supported configurations can use 4 KiB, 16 KiB or 64 KiB. Address width, granule size and table-entry layout together determine the required hierarchy.

Apple’s ARM-based M-series system-on-chip family. macOS on Apple silicon commonly uses 16 KiB pages; the operating-system mapping configuration, rather than the family name alone, determines the granule in a particular environment.
An MMU for devices: it translates the addresses a device uses for DMA, so scattered physical pages can look contiguous to the device and devices can be isolated.
A list of separate memory pieces that a device transfers as one operation, avoiding the need for one contiguous buffer.
Starting exactly on a page boundary: the address is a multiple of the page size. A 2 MiB-aligned address is a multiple of 2 MiB.
Linux's explicit huge-page mechanism: huge pages reserved in advance (for example with vm.nr_hugepages) and used through hugetlbfs or special mmap flags. They are not swapped.
A Linux kernel thread that scans memory and collapses runs of small pages into transparent huge pages in the background.

A transparent-huge-page policy limiting ordinary automatic allocation to advised eligible mappings for sizes inheriting that policy. Per-size and process controls also matter; MADV_COLLAPSE has separate rules and can bypass the global automatic-policy setting.
A TLB hit is an access whose translation is already cached in the TLB; a miss needs another translation cache or a page walk first.
The fraction of a specified set of cache or TLB lookups that hit. The complementary miss rate describes those that miss; entry count alone does not establish either rate.
example: 1,023 hits in 1,024 accesses is a hit rate of about 99.9%.

definition: Effective access time: the average time of one memory access once rare slow cases (TLB misses or page faults) are included, each weighted by how often it happens.
example: With 98% TLB hits at 100 ns and misses at 200 ns, EAT = 0.98 × 100 + 0.02 × 200 = 102 ns.

definition: The tendency for an access pattern to reuse recent data or touch nearby data. Such temporal or spatial locality can help caches and translation caches, but capacity, conflicts and the actual pattern determine hit rates.
The distance in bytes between consecutive memory accesses in a loop. A stride of one page touches a new page on every access.
A TLB whose misses raise an exception so the OS refills it itself, as on MIPS, rather than a hardware page walker doing it.
A RISC processor architecture, notable here for its software-managed TLB and address-space identifiers (ASIDs).
How much memory the TLB can map at once: the number of entries times the page size.
example: 64 entries × 4 KiB = 256 KiB; with 2 MiB pages, 128 MiB.

definition: The part of a workload’s data actively accessed over a relevant interval. Exceeding a cache or TLB’s effective capacity can increase misses, with cost depending on locality, replacement and other hierarchy levels.

An x86 instruction used to invalidate translation information for a page on the executing logical processor, under architectural scope rules. It is not by itself a broadcast invalidation of every other CPU’s TLB.
State maintained separately for logical CPUs, often to reduce shared-state contention. Migration, cross-CPU access and the particular synchronisation protocol still matter.
Performance monitoring unit: CPU hardware that counts events such as cache and TLB misses for tools like perf.
How many places in a cache (or TLB) a given entry may occupy. More ways mean fewer conflicts between entries that map to the same set.

A cache using a virtual-address-derived set index and a physical tag. Common L1 designs choose index bits within the page offset so translation and indexing can overlap; other VIPT organisations need additional alias handling.
The computer scientist whose 1968 paper formalised the working-set model of program behaviour, relating a process’s recently used information to its memory needs.
The x86 page-fault exception (number 14), raised when a translation fails or breaks a permission bit. The CPU stores the address in CR2 and pushes an error code.
A number reporting what went wrong. On a page fault the x86 CPU pushes one whose bits say what happened: P (page was present), W (write), U (from user mode), I (instruction fetch).
example: Error code 0x7 means a user-mode write to a present page: a protection fault, as in copy-on-write.

definition: An instruction whose faulting access can resume or retry after the kernel resolves the fault. The program can still observe latency, counters or a failure signal; restartability does not make faults unobservable.

Virtual memory area: the Linux kernel's record of one mapped region of a process (start, end, permissions and backing file or none). Page-fault handling checks it to decide whether an access is legal.
Memory whose contents come from a file, such as mapped executables and libraries. Clean file pages can be dropped and reread from the file.

A fault arising when an eligible anonymous mapping first needs zero-filled backing. A write commonly obtains private zero-filled backing, while a read can use shared zero backing; accounting and costs depend on the actual path.

A fault accounted as not requiring the page-in I/O associated with a major fault, such as mapping resident backing or first-touch anonymous backing. Allocation, reclaim or contention can still make its handler expensive.

A fault accounted as requiring page-in I/O, for example to obtain missing file or swap backing. Its duration depends on the backing, cache, storage and contention; the label does not promise a fixed delay.
The fraction of accesses causing a specified kind of page fault. Its performance effect depends jointly on that rate and the complete costs of faulting and ordinary accesses.
The kernel reading more of a file than was asked for, expecting sequential access, so later reads find the data already in the page cache.

A Linux optimisation that can install nearby already-resident file-page mappings during a fault. Its window and applicability depend on kernel settings and mapping state, so it need not map a fixed surrounding range.
Filling a mapping's page tables in advance (for example with MAP_POPULATE) instead of waiting for first-touch faults.

Currently backed by resident physical memory. A mapping can exist without resident backing, for example before population or while swapped; resident mapping counts and shared zero-page accounting have additional details.
The Unix error code for an input/output error, returned by interfaces such as read when applicable. A mapped load has no ordinary error return; unresolved backing errors may instead deliver SIGBUS.
The Unix error code meaning 'cannot allocate memory', returned by calls such as mmap and fork when the kernel refuses an allocation.
Lightning Memory-Mapped Database: an embedded key-value store that reads data directly through mmap.
Periodically renaming, truncating or deleting log files so they do not grow forever; truncating a file another process has mapped can cause SIGBUS.

The persistence guarantee that acknowledged data survives the failures covered by a storage protocol. File mapping use may require successful msync or fsync and, for namespace changes, directory synchronisation, with filesystem and hardware guarantees still relevant.
Disk (or compressed RAM) space where the kernel stores anonymous and shared-memory (tmpfs) pages it evicts from RAM, so they can be read back on a later fault.
The location of a swapped-out page (which swap device, which slot), stored by Linux in the page's now not-present PTE.
Linux's cache of pages that are being moved to or from swap, which lets a fault find a swapped page still in RAM without a disk read.
A Linux setting (default 60, range 0 to 200) that biases reclaim between swapping anonymous pages and dropping page cache. 0 strongly prefers dropping cache but does not forbid swapping.

The operation that disables a swap area and attempts to remove its live entries, obtaining suitable backing elsewhere. It can fail under memory pressure and does not promise that the whole area always fits immediately in free RAM.

A compressed-memory cache for swap-backed pages, in front of a swap device. Compression, pool limits, eviction, writeback and fault handling follow configured policy; it does not replace all backing-device requirements.
A Linux compressed block device in RAM, commonly used as swap; it can optionally write pages back to a real device.
A Linux mechanism that lets a user-space program handle page faults on a region of memory itself.
An open-source machine emulator and virtualiser; it uses userfaultfd for post-copy live migration of virtual machines.
Moving a running virtual machine to another host. In post-copy mode it starts on the new host first and fetches memory pages over the network as they fault.
The system call that reports a process's resource usage, including its minor and major page-fault counts.
A C library call that reports system settings; sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) returns the base page size.
Redis’s RDB snapshot file format, representing a dataset at a point in time. BGSAVE normally writes it in a forked child; SAVE is a blocking foreground alternative.
A server that loads its code once and then forks worker processes, which share the loaded pages through copy-on-write.
A pre-fork Python web server: a master process forks a number of worker processes.
PHP's FastCGI process manager, which runs PHP code in a pool of forked worker processes.
Android's pre-forked process that loads the common runtime and libraries once; each app process is forked from it.
A Linux open flag for I/O that bypasses the page cache, subject to alignment rules.
A call giving the kernel hints about how a file will be used; POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED says cached pages may be dropped.
Writing modified (dirty) pages from memory to their file or swap so the frames can be reused.
Choosing which resident page to evict when a page fault needs a free frame and none is left. Good choices evict pages that will not be needed for a long time.
The page a replacement policy chooses to evict. In OOM handling, the victim is the process chosen to be killed.
The sequence of page numbers a program touches, used to compare replacement policies by counting the faults each causes.
example: The string 1 2 3 1 4 1 2 5 with 3 frames gives 7 faults under FIFO and 6 under LRU.

definition: A first-use miss in a model starting with empty memory and no prefetching. A replacement policy cannot turn that initial absent reference into a hit under those assumptions.
Belady's optimal page replacement: evict the page whose next use is furthest in the future. It gives the fewest faults possible but needs to know the future, so it serves only as a yardstick.
The surprising case where giving FIFO more frames causes more page faults on some reference strings. Stack algorithms such as LRU and OPT cannot suffer it.
example: 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 gives 9 FIFO faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4.

definition: A replacement policy whose resident set at one frame budget remains a subset of the set at a larger budget, so adding frames cannot add faults. LRU has this property; the standard OPT stack formulation uses consistent tie handling, while FIFO does not.
A replacement policy's ability to keep hot pages when a large one-pass sequential scan, such as a backup, flows through memory.

An approximation of LRU: frames sit in a circle and a hand sweeps round; a page with its accessed bit set has the bit cleared and is skipped once, and the first page found with the bit clear is evicted.
A clock variant that also looks at the dirty bit, preferring unused clean pages, then unused dirty, then used clean, then used dirty.

Linux’s classic reclaim organisation separating active and inactive lists for anonymous and file backing. Observed reuse, refault feedback and access-path exceptions influence admission and promotion; inactive lists are candidates rather than guaranteed immediate victims.
The kernel's index from a physical page back to every PTE that maps it, so reclaim can check accessed bits and unmap shared pages.

A later reference to backing after eviction. Linux refault tracking can retain shadow information and compare eviction-distance history to working-set size; this is not simply elapsed wall-clock time.
Multi-generational LRU: a Linux page-reclaim design (from Linux 6.1, by Google) that sorts pages into several age generations instead of two lists.
A range of physical memory that Linux manages separately, for example ZONE_NORMAL; each has its own free lists and watermarks.

Zone free-memory thresholds used in allocation and reclaim decisions. Falling below low can wake kswapd towards high; allocation flags, order, fragmentation, memory-cgroup limits and other rules affect direct reclaim.
The Linux kernel thread that reclaims memory in the background when free memory falls below the low watermark.
The kernel freeing page frames by dropping clean cache pages, writing back dirty ones and swapping anonymous memory.

Reclaim work performed in an allocating task’s context on a permitted allocation path. It can add latency, but may fail to free enough memory; not every allocation or low-watermark condition enters it.

Linux tunables influencing free-memory watermarks and their spacing. They can change when background reclaim wakes and how much reserve is maintained; effects depend on memory zones, workload and configuration.
A state where the active working sets exceed memory, so pages are evicted and refaulted constantly and the system spends its time moving pages rather than running programs.
A control scheme that gives a process more frames when its fault rate is high and takes some away when it is low.
CPU time recorded as idle while some task waits for I/O. It is an unreliable sign of thrashing on its own.
Pressure stall information: Linux's measure of the share of time tasks were stalled waiting for memory (or CPU or I/O). 'some' means at least one task stalled; 'full' means all non-idle tasks did.

Meta’s user-space workload-killing daemon using configurable policies and pressure signals such as PSI. It can act before kernel OOM, but earlier action is not guaranteed for every policy or workload.
The systemd service that kills cgroups under sustained memory pressure or swap use, according to configured policy.
A small user-space daemon that kills the process with the highest score when available memory and swap drop below thresholds.
In strict overcommit mode, the percentage of RAM counted towards CommitLimit (default 50); overcommit_kbytes gives an absolute amount instead when nonzero.

The strict-overcommit accounting limit shown in /proc/meminfo, combining swap with either a configured usable-RAM ratio or an absolute RAM contribution. HugeTLB reservation and admission reserves affect the complete accounting rules.
example: 64 GiB of RAM, 8 GiB of swap and ratio 50 give 8 + 32 = 40 GiB.

definition: The system-wide accounted commitment shown in /proc/meminfo. Strict admission uses this accounting together with CommitLimit and applicable reserves; it is not a measurement of resident memory.
A Linux file reporting system-wide memory figures such as MemAvailable, CommitLimit, Committed_AS and Slab.

A per-process setting (/proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj) from −1000 to +1000 added to its OOM badness score; each unit is worth one-thousandth of the allowed memory, and −1000 exempts the process from the OOM killer.

A read-only per-process file showing the OOM killer's current score for that process, including oom_score_adj. It is a rescaled form of the badness score, shifted so it is never negative; a higher value means the process is more likely to be killed.
The score the OOM killer uses to choose a victim: roughly the process's resident, swapped and page-table memory as a share of the allowance, plus oom_score_adj.
example: 6 GiB of a 16 GiB allowance scores about 375; 2 GiB with +500 scores about 625.

definition: The command that prints the kernel's log ring buffer, where OOM kills and other kernel events are recorded.
Virtual size: the total size of all of a process's mappings, touched or not. Shown as VSZ by ps and VIRT by top; it says little about RAM use.

Resident mapped memory apportioned by each backing page’s sharing count. Summing across all relevant sharers approximates the represented resident mappings, with rounding and accounting caveats; it excludes unrelated kernel memory and unmapped cache.
example: 40 MiB private plus a quarter of 100 MiB shared is a PSS of 65 MiB.

definition: Unique set size: the resident memory private to one process.
Linux files giving per-mapping (smaps) or totalled (smaps_rollup) memory figures for a process, including Rss, Pss and swap.
Fields of /proc/<pid>/status splitting a process's RSS into anonymous memory, file-backed memory and shared memory (shmem).
A tool that reports PSS and USS for processes, giving a fairer picture of shared memory than RSS.
The kernel's estimate of how much memory could be given to new work without swapping, including reclaimable page cache. More useful than 'free'.
The command that prints total, used, free and available memory; its 'free' column excludes cache and so looks alarmingly low on a healthy machine.
The cgroup v2 controller that charges a group's anonymous memory, page cache and much kernel memory, and enforces memory.min, memory.low, memory.high and memory.max.
The cgroup v2 file showing the group's current memory charge, page cache included.
The cgroup v2 hard memory limit. A group at the limit reclaims, and if that fails, may OOM-kill within the group.

The cgroup v2 boundary above which eligible tasks are throttled and perform reclaim. Crossing it does not itself invoke kernel OOM; independent pressure, ancestor limits or a user-space killer can still terminate tasks.

Cgroup v2 reclaim protection settings: memory.min supplies hard protection within the effective ancestor budget, while memory.low is best effort. Protection overcommitment and ancestor limits affect what a child actually receives.
A cgroup v2 file counting events such as high, max, oom and oom_kill; the first place to look after a container dies.
A cgroup v2 file breaking the group's memory into categories such as anon, file, kernel and shmem.
A cgroup v2 setting requesting that OOM handling treat a workload as a group for killing. Scope rules and exemptions such as oom_score_adj at minus one thousand still apply.
The Kubernetes agent on each node that starts and stops containers. Under node memory pressure it can evict pods, separately from the kernel OOM killer.
The reason Kubernetes reports when a container's process was killed for an out-of-memory condition, usually with exit code 137.

Kubernetes container requests guide scheduling, while memory limits normally configure the runtime’s cgroup memory constraint. On cgroup v2 that limit is represented by memory.max; optional protections and ancestor limits add policy.

A Kubernetes feature using cgroup v2 memory controls for additional protection or throttling derived from requests and limits. Availability, feature-gate status and exact controller behaviour are version-dependent; inspect the deployed cluster.
A Kubernetes scratch volume that lives as long as the pod; with medium: Memory it is a tmpfs in RAM that counts against the memory limit.
JVM options sizing the Java heap: -Xmx sets the maximum heap directly; MaxRAMPercentage sets it as a share of the detected container or machine memory.
The JVM's native memory area for class metadata, outside the Java heap.

A HotSpot JVM feature that reports tracked internal VM memory by category, including Java heap reservations and native categories. It does not account for every third-party native allocation, JDK class-library allocation or cgroup charge.
A snapshot of every object on a managed runtime's heap, used to see what is using memory.
Google's compiled, garbage-collected programming language. GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19+) sets a soft memory budget for its runtime.
AddressSanitizer: compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=address) that detects out-of-bounds and use-after-free bugs at run time.

LeakSanitizer reports detected unreachable heap allocations, commonly at process exit on supported platforms. It integrates with AddressSanitizer in supported Linux configurations and can be disabled or configured, so every build need not emit the same report.
A heap profiler for Linux that records every allocation with its call stack.
A bcc tool that uses eBPF to attach to allocation functions in a running process and report allocations still outstanding, by stack.
Python's standard module that traces memory allocations and compares snapshots to show which lines allocated the most.
A tool that records where live memory was allocated, revealing structures that keep growing even while still reachable.
A glibc diagnostic reporting usable capacity associated with an allocation, which can exceed its requested size. This does not permit an application to write beyond the original requested allocation.
example: malloc(100) in the lesson's glibc model reports 104 usable bytes.

definition: How an allocator picks a free block for a request: first fit takes the first big-enough hole, best fit the smallest one that fits, segregated fits use a list per size class.
Keeping separate free lists for different size classes, so a request is served quickly from the matching list at the cost of some rounding waste.
One of the fixed sizes an allocator rounds requests up to, each with its own free list or slabs.
example: In jemalloc a 257-byte request goes in the 320-byte size class.

definition: Merging adjacent free blocks into one larger block, which reduces external fragmentation.

glibc malloc’s allocation unit, with size/status metadata and user storage. In the lesson’s ordinary glibc 2.39 x86-64 model chunks are sixteen-byte multiples with a thirty-two-byte minimum; separately mapped chunks and other configurations differ.
The malloc implementations glibc's allocator descends from: Doug Lea's dlmalloc, extended for threads as ptmalloc2.

A per-thread cache of recently freed small chunks in glibc malloc (2.26 onwards; with the 2.39 defaults, 64 size classes holding up to 7 chunks each), giving malloc and free a lock-free fast path. Other allocators have similar per-thread caches.
glibc lists of small freed chunks that are kept unmerged so they can be reused quickly.

glibc free-chunk structures include an unsorted staging bin, exact-size small bins and size-ordered large bins. Some freed chunks instead enter tcache or fastbins, so freeing does not imply immediate unsorted-bin insertion or coalescing.
In glibc malloc, the free space at the end of an arena's heap, from which new chunks are split when no bin fits.

Allocator state with its own chunk-management structures and synchronisation. In the stated glibc 2.39 64-bit model the ordinary default arena cap is eight times online CPUs; jemalloc’s documented defaults and tunables differ.

glibc’s M_TRIM_THRESHOLD controls when eligible top free space can trigger automatic trimming, subject to allocator state and settings. malloc_trim is a separate explicit call that can release suitable whole free pages, including some internal free regions.
An environment variable capping how many glibc malloc arenas a process creates; lower values can cut memory retention at the cost of lock contention.
Functions reporting an allocator's internal state, including memory freed but retained: malloc_stats in glibc, mallctl in jemalloc.

A malloc implementation grouping small objects by size class in slabs, with thread caching, arenas and configurable page decay. Statistics and heap profiling depend on the build and runtime configuration.
Google's allocator, with per-CPU (or per-thread) caches, central free lists and a huge-page-aware page heap.
Microsoft Research's compact allocator, which uses free-list sharding: many small free lists per page for locality and a very short fast path.
mimalloc's technique of keeping many small free lists, one set per page, instead of one big list per size class.
A Linux feature that lets a short per-CPU code sequence be restarted if the thread is preempted or migrated, giving lock-free per-CPU data without atomic instructions.
Layers inside tcmalloc: transfer caches move batches of objects between CPUs, central free lists track spans (runs of pages holding one size class), and the page heap manages the pages themselves.
jemalloc's policy of returning unused pages to the OS gradually over time, rather than immediately or never.
An environment variable telling the Linux dynamic linker to load given libraries first, which can swap in a different malloc for a dynamically linked program.

An optional CPython allocator using pools within arenas for small requests up to 512 bytes in standard GIL-enabled configurations. Free-threaded builds require mimalloc, and settings or extension code can use other allocation paths.
Writing past the end of a heap-allocated buffer, which can corrupt neighbouring objects or the allocator's in-band metadata and is a common route to exploits.
Freeing memory on a different thread from the one that allocated it, which complicates per-thread caches.

The Linux kernel's physical page allocator. It keeps free blocks of 2^k pages per order, splits bigger blocks in half to satisfy requests, and merges a freed block with its equal-sized neighbour (its buddy), found by XOR.
example: A 12 KiB request gets an order-2 (16 KiB) block, wasting 4 KiB.

definition: The size class of a buddy block: an order-k block is 2^k contiguous pages, so order 0 is 4 KiB and order 9 is 2 MiB with 4 KiB pages.
A Linux file listing, for each memory zone, how many free blocks of each order there are.

An object-cache allocation design described by Jeff Bonwick for Solaris in 1994. Slabs divide backing pages into fixed-size slots; metadata, alignment, hardening and debugging can add overhead even without a malloc-style size header on every live object.
Linux's slab allocator implementations: SLUB is the default and, since SLOB was removed in 6.4 and SLAB in 6.8, the only one.
The Linux kernel's general-purpose small-object allocator, built on slab caches of fixed sizes (8, 16, 32 ... bytes).
A tool (reading /proc/slabinfo) that shows how much memory each kernel slab cache uses.
Directory entry: the kernel's in-memory record linking a file name to the file's metadata, cached in large numbers in a slab cache to speed up path lookups.
The Linux kernel's per-thread (task) record, allocated from a slab cache.
Exclusive or: a bitwise operation whose result bit is 1 when exactly one of the two input bits is 1. XOR with a single-bit value flips that bit.
Placing data at an address that is a multiple of some size, as hardware or allocators require. A 64 KiB-aligned block starts at a multiple of 64 KiB.
A number 2^k: 1, 2, 4, 8 ... Memory sizes, page sizes and buddy blocks are powers of two, which makes splitting addresses into fields a matter of cutting bits.
A number written in base 2, using only the digits 0 and 1; each digit is one bit.
Floor (written ⌊x⌋) rounds a number down to a whole number; ceiling (⌈x⌉) rounds it up.

A logarithm asks which exponent produces a positive value from a chosen base. For example, the base-two logarithm of eight is three. Choosing among a non-power-of-two number of items requires rounding up to a whole bit count.

Moving an integer’s bits left or right, using operators such as << and >>. For nonnegative values, shifting right discards low bits and rounds division by the corresponding power of two down; signed and overflow rules depend on the language. Bit masks retain selected positions, while AND and OR combine bits under different rules.
Linux kernel settings that can be read and changed at run time, such as vm.swappiness (in /proc/sys); sysfs (/sys) exposes further settings such as the THP policy.
Occupying consecutive physical frames. Ordinary pages need not be; huge pages and some device buffers must be.
Turning a virtual address into a physical one, done by the MMU using page tables and cached in the TLB.
The Unix command that lists processes and their statistics, such as VSZ, RSS and page-fault counts.

Running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine so another guest can execute within it. Additional translation and exit machinery can add overhead, but its size depends on hardware support, caching, configuration and workload.
The PostgreSQL setting that asks for explicit huge pages (HugeTLB) for its main shared-memory region.

The x86 registers that select segments: CS (code), DS (data), ES (extra), SS (stack), and FS and GS. In 64-bit mode the CPU treats the bases of CS, DS, ES and SS as 0; only the FS and GS bases still matter, used for thread-local storage and per-CPU data.

One particular route through the kernel's code, taken in some circumstances: the fault path handles page faults, an allocation path runs when memory is requested, and some reclaim paths free memory while others make an allocation fail at once.
A page the kernel must keep at its current physical location, typically because a device or kernel code holds a reference for direct I/O. It cannot be moved, swapped or reclaimed while pinned.
A distance, usually in bytes, from the start of something: a page (the page offset), a segment, a file (the file offset) or a packet. Adding it to the start gives the position of the item it names.
example: Address 0x3A7C is offset 0xA7C into page 3.

definition: A saved record or preserved view of some state as it was at one moment: for example a Redis dataset written by a forked child, a tracemalloc record of allocations, a read-only view of a file system (often kept cheaply by copy-on-write), or a virtual machine's disk and memory. Container tools such as containerd also call a prepared file-system layer stack a snapshot.

Data that describes other data rather than being its content, such as a malloc chunk's size header, a slab's free list, a file's size, permissions and block locations (held in inodes and directories), or a network packet's length and protocol.
The logging service of systemd, read with journalctl, where services such as systemd-oomd record what they did.
The resident-memory column in top: the same quantity as RSS, the process's pages currently in RAM, counting shared pages in full.
The x86-64 control-register flag (and CPU feature) that enables 5-level paging, giving 57-bit virtual addresses.

Invalidating some or all cached translations according to the chosen operation and architecture. Ordinary CR3 writes without PCIDs invalidate relevant non-global entries; enabled global mappings and other scope rules prevent treating every such write as an unconditional whole-TLB flush.

The goal that ordinary programs use their own virtual addresses without managing physical placement themselves. The OS and hardware provide translation, although faults, limits and performance remain observable.
The goal of keeping virtual-memory translation fast and its metadata reasonably small. TLBs reduce translation work while sparse page tables avoid storing entries for unused regions.

Restricting which mapped memory a process can access and which operations it may perform. The OS establishes mappings and permissions; ordinary user-mode access instructions cannot bypass the applicable hardware checks.
